analysis.one_liner: Extends children's online privacy law to teens and bans tracking them for targeted ads.
analysis.headline: The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved the bill by voice vote in September 2024, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill updates the 1998 children's online privacy law to cover teens up to age 17, not just young children. It would ban apps and websites from collecting kids' and teens' personal data to target them with individualized ads, cover new data types like geolocation and biometric identifiers, give teens and parents the right to see and delete collected data, and require companies to protect that data from breaches. It also preserves the ability of states to pass stronger protections. It never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, whose personal data, location, biometric identifiers, and online profiles would be protected from collection and use for targeted advertising; parents, who would gain notice and consent rights and the ability to review and delete their child's data; and states, which could add stronger protections of their own.

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends the existing children's online privacy law from children under 13 to teens ages 13 to 16, covering a far larger group of users whose data companies could otherwise collect and sell [S2].

It makes it unlawful for operators to collect, use, or disclose a child's or teen's personal information for individualized advertising, and defines that term to cover profiling based on a young person's data or a device identifier [S2].

It expands the definition of personal information to include geolocation, photographs and voice files, biometric identifiers like facial templates and DNA, and persistent identifiers like IP addresses that track a user across sites and apps [S2].
It gives teens, not just parents, the right to see what data a company collected, delete their information and posts, and correct inaccurate data [S2].

It requires operators to maintain reasonable security practices to protect children's and teens' data from unauthorized access, and to delete it once it is no longer needed for the requested service [S2].
The bill replaces broad federal preemption with a conflicts-only rule, expressly allowing states to enact stronger protections for children and teens [S2].
It requires the Federal Trade Commission to report annually on its enforcement of the law, including the number of investigations and complaints, creating public accountability [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Online platforms, app developers, and the advertising technology industry, which would lose the ability to build profiles of minors and serve them targeted ads, and would bear the cost of compliance, notices, deletion systems, and security measures. Small developers get a lighter-touch analysis requirement but still face compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Social media platforms and ad-tech companies

drawbacks.text: The bill does not require companies to verify users' ages: it expressly says operators need not implement age-gating or age-verification, relying instead on 'knowledge fairly implied on the basis of objective circumstances,' which could let platforms claim ignorance that a user is a minor [S2].

The FTC's guidance on how that knowledge standard will be applied is expressly non-binding and cannot be the basis of an enforcement action, which may make enforcement inconsistent and litigable [S2].

Compliance costs fall on all covered operators, and the bill requires regulators to analyze the impact on small entities, acknowledging that smaller app developers could face a disproportionate burden [S2].

The bill allows operators working under agreements with schools to collect student data without parental consent, provided the data is limited to educational purposes — a carve-out that shifts oversight to school administrators [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families, the benefits are substantial: fewer ads built on children's profiles, deletion rights, and stronger data security, while the main cost is compliance spending by platforms and apps. The design has real gaps — no age verification and non-binding FTC guidance — but the core restrictions on profiling minors are meaningful, and states may go further. The larger failure is procedural: a bill with bipartisan support that cleared committee was never allowed a floor vote.

outcome.mechanism: The Energy and Commerce Committee approved the bill in September 2024, but House leaders never brought it to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Tim Walberg introduced the bill on April 9, 2024, with bipartisan original cosponsors including Democrats Kathy Castor and Anna Eshoo, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1, S2].
The bill gathered 28 cosponsors split 16 Democrats and 12 Republicans [S3].
On September 18, 2024, the committee held a markup session and ordered the bill reported to the House with amendments by voice vote [S4].
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a vote in the full House and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online platforms and the advertising technology industry are better off: the bill that would have restricted collecting and profiling minors' data for targeted advertising died without a floor vote, so the status quo remains.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship and support throughout: a Republican sponsor, 28 cosponsors split 16 Democrats and 12 Republicans, and approval by voice vote in committee, with no recorded opposition in the congressional record.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful to collect, use, or disclose minors' personal information for individualized advertising, striking at the profiling-based ad model. Its gain had been a constant stream of young users' data at no cost to the industry.

industries.industry: Social media platforms and app developers
industries.note: The bill covers mobile and online apps, not just websites, and adds duties: notices, deletion and correction rights for teens, data-retention limits, and security requirements. These costs fall on platforms, while the restrictions protect the young users those platforms court.

The bill lets operators collecting student data under school agreements proceed without parental consent, so long as use is limited to educational purposes. This locks in ed-tech companies' role as the channel for student data in schools, with oversight shifted to school administrators rather than parents.

industries.industry: State attorneys general and consumer enforcement
industries.note: The bill expands state attorneys general enforcement to the new restrictions and expressly preserves states' power to enact stronger protections for children and teens.
